definition: Aversion means a particular dislike for something.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word aversion. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know aversion should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Even as a kitten she showed a marked aversion to the vacuum cleaner, relocating to the top shelf at the first click of its cord.
Distaste registers and moves on — you finish the meeting anyway; an aversion redraws the route.
Disgust goes past aversion: the turning-away has become physical, a recoil you can see.

Reluctance is unwillingness to take a particular action — you hang back from the next step, and duty or nerves can cause it without any dislike at all. An aversion is a settled dislike of the thing itself, and it steers the whole route: detours, refusals, itineraries bent around the airport. Reluctance drags one foot; an aversion redraws the map.

Dread is fear pointed at the future — the cold weight of something coming that you cannot stop. An aversion needn't be afraid at all: the director laughs about flying; she simply never boards a plane. Dread braces for the thing; an aversion calmly arranges never to meet it.

Aversion means a particular dislike for something.
The film director's aversion to flying is part of festival legend.
She has crossed to Cannes by freighter, taken four trains to Venice, and once judged a Sydney festival entirely over video link.
Ask her about it and she laughs; book her a flight and her office quietly books the sleeper car instead.
Aversion is the exact word because it names a particular dislike — and one that behaves.
An aversion doesn't just disapprove; it steers.
The word's Latin bones mean a turning-away, and that is precisely what her itineraries do: whatever the route, it bends around the airport.
Aversion is the dislike that steers: it shows up as detours, refusals, and empty seats near the thing avoided.
Its cluster-mate in this unit, antipathy, runs deeper and argues its case; an aversion mostly just leaves the room.
Keep dread for fear — an aversion can be perfectly calm about the thing it never goes near.

Ito has built a career on plants, yet her colleagues know one green thing she cannot stand: the lawn.
Her aversion is not fear and not squeamishness; she will happily walk across a lawn to reach an interesting weed.
But she has never planted one, and her own yard is a mosaic of moss, clover, and wild thyme.
Asked about it, she calmly lists her reasons -- thirsty, fussy, biologically empty -- the way a judge reads a verdict.
Friends have learned to route garden-club tours around the turf exhibits, because her settled dislike quietly redraws every itinerary she is part of.
